title: Hierarchical admission shaper for dedicated routing and overload protection
creator: Aisha Nadar
description: Background: Dedicated pools must provide throughput guarantees while protecting the fleet from overload. Current admission behavior is coarse: simple per-pod rate limits and global shedding rules lead to unfairness across tenants, poor tail latency under transient spikes, and inefficient autoscaler signals. Goal: implement a hierarchical admission shaper (HAS) that combines per-tenant token buckets, model-cost-aware admission, and a short wait-queue with prioritized dequeueing. HAS should coordinate with the autoscaler so sustained queue build-up triggers scale decisions while short spikes are absorbed without unnecessary scale-ups. Deliverables: design + implementation of admission shaper, integration tests, load-test evidence, rollout runbook, and console metrics/dashboards.
acceptance_criteria: Per-tenant throughput enforcement: tenants with reserved capacity maintain configured RPS during sustained load (95th percentile within 5% of target)
Fairness: lower-priority tenants are throttled/preempted before higher-priority tenants when pool capacity is saturated
Autoscaler integration: sustained queue depth > threshold for 30s triggers scale-up signal; queue draining after scale-down avoids immediate preemption
Observability: per-tenant admitted/denied counts, average queue wait, backpressure reasons, and estimated cost-per-request exposed in console
Graceful overload behavior: short spikes result in queued waits with Retry-After guidance; long overloads result in early shedding with informative 429/503 responses and documented retry semantics
updates: 2025-02-12 - Created ticket. Initial notes on goals and constraints; flagged dependency on autoscaler metrics API (ENG-12980).

2025-02-19 - Design spike completed: simulated hierarchical token bucket + small FIFO wait-queue improved p95 tail by ~18% in synthetic bursts (link to simulation dashboard). Decision: keep short max-queue time (200ms) to avoid long-tail latency for real-time apps.

2025-02-25 - Trade-off discussion: early-drop vs aggressive queueing. Chose hybrid: attempt short queueing for up to 200ms, then shed based on tenant priority and model cost. Documented rationale in design doc.

2025-03-01 - Implementation: admission controller core + per-tenant bucket and model-cost estimator wired. Added metrics for admitted, queued, dropped split by reason. PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4587

2025-03-05 - Integration tests added for per-tenant reservations and preemption semantics. Found race where autoscaler saw transient queue spike from canary traffic; added smoothing window to scale signal (30s).
notes: Key algorithm: hierarchical token buckets (global -> tenant -> route), admission score = tenant_weight * reserved_tokens - model_cost_estimate. Requests scored negatively may be queued briefly or shed. Must ensure deterministic ordering for canary/critical routes. Backpressure responses include structured JSON with fields: reason, retry_after_seconds, fallback_model_suggestion (if available).
rollout_plan: 1) Feature flag behind env var per-cluster. 2) Canary on a small dedicated pool with low-risk tenants for 48h. 3) Monitor queue depth, admitted/dropped ratio, p95 latency; gradually enable on additional pools. 4) If violations detected, flip flag off and roll back autoscaler smoothing to previous behavior.
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Overly aggressive shedding could break latency-sensitive customers. Mitigation: default policy is permissive with short queueing and only shed when sustained overload and clear priority differences.
Risk: Autoscaler feedback loop from short-lived queues causing oscillation. Mitigation: use 30s smoothing window and require sustained signal before scale-up; implement cooldown after scale events.
Risk: Complexity in correctness under multi-node token accounting. Mitigation: use lease-based local tokens with occasional reconciliation and conservative safety margin to avoid over-admission.
Risk: Customers misinterpret 429 vs 503. Mitigation: standardize response payload and update API docs and SDK error classes to surface retry semantics and suggested fallbacks.
